segments.text: 6 Minute English from bbclearningenglish.com

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Phil.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: And I'm Pippa. Have you ever phoned up a company and had your call held in a queue?

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: If you have, then you've probably heard messages like this.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Hello, your call is important to us. You are number 89 in the queue.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: If you'd like to continue to hold press 1, if you'd like to return to the main menu, press 0.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: How do you feel when your phone call is put on hold, Phil?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Oh, frustrated usually.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Although, I do like it when there's a number saying how many people are in front of you.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: That's good.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Well, when your call is finally connected, it's usually a call centre worker you'll speak to,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: a real live person who'll hopefully fix your problem.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: but increasingly this work is now done using artificial intelligence or AI

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: and this is causing problems in countries like India and the Philippines

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: where call centre jobs make up a big part of the economy.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: In this programme we'll be asking who's really in charge at the call centre, humans or AI?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: As always we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and remember you can read along with the programme

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and find the list of new words and phrases by visiting our website bbclearningenglish

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: But now I have a question for you Phil Around the world numbers of call centre workers have grown rapidly in recent years If you listening to this maybe you a call centre worker yourself

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: So approximately how many people work in call centres globally, Phil?

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Is it A, 7 million, B, 17 million or C, 27 million?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Ooh, I think B, 17 million.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: OK, well, you'll have to listen to the end to find out the answer.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Now, one worker worried about the impact of AI on jobs in the Philippines is Mylene Cabilona,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: president of the call centre workers union, BIEN.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Here, she tells BBC World Service programme Tech Life about some of the difficulties of her job

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: and why she fears for the future.

segments.speaker: Mylene Cabalona
segments.text: So, and this person is quite already aggravated and he keeps on yelling.

segments.speaker: Mylene Cabalona
segments.text: And that's the, you know, that's the difficult part because the mental stress also, you know, you have to pacify the client and you have to make sure you're able to resolve the concern.

segments.speaker: Mylene Cabalona
segments.text: And then the difficult part on that conversation is that you're being monitored by an AI.

segments.speaker: Mylene Cabalona
segments.text: I mean, eventually AI would replace us.

segments.speaker: Mylene Cabalona
segments.text: It's going to displace workers in the, you know, eventually in the near future.

segments.speaker: Mylene Cabalona
segments.text: Even as a matter of fact there been a study that says that about 300 workers or around 27 of workers that going to be displaced because of AI And that slowly happening

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Call centre work involves dealing with customers who've phoned up to complain.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: They're often angry, aggravated and yelling or shouting down the phone.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: It's Mylene's job to pacify them, to calm them down.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: If that wasn't stressful enough,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Mylene's conversations are monitored by AI systems to see how well she fixes her clients' problems.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: You might think AI was built to support workers like Mylene,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: but she fears AI will replace her in the near future,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: a phrase meaning very soon or within a short time.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Mylene emphasises her fears about being replaced by giving details about a study she read

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: which claimed that 27% of workers will be displaced by AI.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: She uses the phrase as a matter of fact to emphasise what she's saying and to give more detail as evidence to support it.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: But Mylene thinks AI will never fully replace humans.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: She says AI lacks one important quality, empathy.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Here she explains more to BBC World Service's Tech Life.

segments.speaker: Mylene Cabalona
segments.text: Well, I don't think AI is empathetic or whenever they talk.

segments.speaker: Mylene Cabalona
segments.text: I mean, if ever a machine or a robot talks to them, you know, people are more compassionate than, you know, when you talk to a robot.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Mylene says that AI is not empathetic Unlike humans it can put itself in someone else place and share their feelings or experiences

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: If you listen carefully to Mylene speech

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: you'll notice she says, you know a lot. Phrases like, you know, um, and are are called filler

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: words and are used to give the speaker time to think or to express uncertainty. Right,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: I think it's time I revealed the answer to my question, Phil.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: I asked you how many call centre workers are there globally.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And I said 17 million.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Which is the right answer.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learned in this programme,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: starting with yelling, another word for shouting.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: To pacify someone means to calm them down when they're angry.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: In the near future means very soon or within a short time.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The phrase, as a matter of fact, is used to add emphasis to what you're saying,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: to give more detail about what you've just said, or to introduce something that contrasts with it.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: If you're empathetic, you're able to put yourself in someone else's position and share their feelings or experiences.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And finally, filler words like, um, ah, and you know, give the speaker more time to think or to express uncertainty.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up. Bye!

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Bye!
